newsitem.title: LEBANON: Syrian troops abandon landmark Beirut positions.
newsitem.headline: Syrian troops abandon landmark Beirut positions.

text.p: Syrian troops have pulled out in the past few days from several landmark positions they have occupied for years in and around Beirut, witnesses said on Thursday.
It was not immediately possible to confirm whether the moves were part of a redeployment of forces or a permanent thinning of the Syrian military presence in the Lebanese capital.
Syria has an estimated 35,000 troops stationed across two-thirds of Lebanon.

Last month, Syrian troops also left a number of positions in the central Lebanese mountains, in what Lebanese security sources said was a defensive redeployment following apparent Israeli threats to attack Syrian forces in Lebanon.
On Thursday morning half a dozen trucks piled high with Syrian soldiers, bedding and furniture moved north along the seafront Corniche promenade in west Beirut.

A large tent encampment overlooking the Corniche near the Beirut lighthouse a few hundred metres (yards) further south was gone. The camp had been one of the most visible symbols of the Syrian military presence in Beirut since 1987.

The Syrians also abandoned camps in two other west Beirut landmarks in the past three days -- the Murr tower, Lebanon's tallest building overlooking a highway linking east and west Beirut, and the bombed-out St Georges Hotel on the coast which was once the city's best-known luxury hotel.
Syrian soldiers were seen moving dozens of ammunition boxes out of the St Georges on Wednesday night and they were gone on Thursday morning.

Residents said the Syrians had also vacated a building next to the Gefinor building, a west Beirut banking and financial centre, in the past week. A checkpoint near the former Green Line civil war battlefront at Ras el-Naba was also vacated.
The conservative Beirut daily an-Nahar said Syrian soldiers had also left positions near the presidential palace at Baabda overlooking Beirut and in the suburbs of Hazmiyeh and Hadath.
Lebanese security sources told Reuters the Syrians had abandoned some of these positions and had reduced their strength at others by 50 percent.
They said owners of buildings and hotels occupied by the Syrians had been asking them to leave.

Despite the pullouts, armed Syrian troops were still stationed in Beirut and the suburbs and were highly visible in some areas, including Shi'ite Moslem suburbs that are a stronghold of the pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God).

Some of the positions they left, including the Murr tower and the St Georges hotel, are awaiting multi-million dollar refurbishments under Lebanon's postwar reconstruction plans which could not begin while the Syrians occupied them.

Syria was scheduled under the 1989 Taef accord which ended Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war to pull its army back from Beirut by 1992. The Lebanese government says the Syrians have stayed on to help it maintain security.
